3	## Overview
4	
5	**Use Case ID:** UC-002   
6	**Use Case Name:** View Veterinarians   
7	**Primary Actor:** Visitor   
8	**Goal:** Browse the list of veterinarians employed at the clinic along with their specialties.   
9	**Status:** Approved

17	
18	1. Visitor clicks the "Veterinarians" link in the navigation bar.
19	2. System retrieves the first set of veterinarians.
20	3. System renders the veterinarians grid showing, for each vet, the first name, last name, and a comma-separated list of
21	   specialties (or "none" if no specialties are held).
22	4. As the Visitor scrolls toward the end of the grid, the system fetches and appends the next chunk of veterinarians

29	**Trigger:** The clinic has no veterinarians recorded (step 2).

3	**Question:** How is the code organized, built, and kept honest?  
4	**Artifacts:** this document, [`testing.md`](testing.md) (the testing half of this
5	view), `CLAUDE.md` (the short form an agent always has loaded)  
6	**Notation:** Markdown  
7	**For the agent:** the most important view, and the one to read **before writing
8	anything** in `src/main/java/`. Every rule here saves a correction in every use
9	case.
10	
11	Most of what follows is **enforced executably** by
12	`src/test/java/ai/unifiedprocess/petclinic/ArchitectureTest.java` (ArchUnit, runs
13	with `./mvnw test`). Each rule names the section it comes from, so a failure
14	points straight back here. If you change a convention below, change the matching
15	rule in the same commit — a rule that contradicts this document is the rule
16	that's wrong.

# Business Rules

Rules that more than one use case must honour.

A rule that belongs to a single use case stays **in** that use case as
`BR-NNN` — it is part of that use case's story and has no life of its own. A
rule that several use cases share lives **here** as `GR-NNN`, is stated once,
and is referenced by each use case that applies it. The use case keeps its local
`BR-NNN` heading, so tests and the traceability sensors still point at a rule of
that use case; the heading says which shared rule it realizes instead of
restating it.

`BusinessRuleTraceabilityTest` (`./mvnw test`) keeps the two sides honest: it
fails when a use case references a rule that does not exist, when a link lands
on a renamed heading, when the `**Realized by:**` line and the use cases
disagree in either direction, when the summary table drifts from the rules below
it, or when a rule here is realized by fewer than two use cases.

**Why `GR` and not `BR`.** `BR-NNN` ids are scoped to a use case: every
`UC-NNN-*.md` numbers its rules from `BR-001`, and `@UseCase(businessRules =
"BR-001")` is resolved inside that one file. A global `BR-001` would therefore
stand beside ten local ones and mean nothing on its own. `GR` — global rule —
is a second namespace precisely so that an id never needs a use case to
disambiguate it.

| Id     | Rule                             | Realized by                                  | From    |
|--------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|---------|
| GR-001 | Anonymous Access                 | UC-001 BR-001, UC-002 BR-003, UC-010 BR-001  | C-010   |
| GR-002 | Lazy Loading of Lists            | UC-002 BR-001, UC-004 BR-002                 | NFR-001, NFR-002 |
| GR-003 | Deterministic Ordering           | UC-002 BR-002, UC-005 BR-001, UC-005 BR-002  | NFR-003 |
| GR-004 | Complete Owner Contact Details   | UC-003 BR-001, UC-006 BR-001                 | FR-005  |
| GR-005 | Telephone Format                 | UC-003 BR-002, UC-006 BR-002
